title: An eye that sees (Avot 2:1)
hook: remember three things above you: an eye that sees, an ear that hears, a book that records

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Judah the Prince, the mother bird, and no price list for good deeds. Your line was small ones count. Which small one did you do with care? Today, the end of the same saying. Day two hundred fifty.

A police car slides into the rearview mirror, and suddenly the whole highway is driving the speed limit. There's a similar gap between the person someone is in public and the person they are alone at eleven at night with a phone. Today's saying is about that gap. It closes the same teaching of Rabbi Judah the Prince we started yesterday. He gives three things to keep in mind so you won't stumble. They're short. You could fit them on a sticky note on your fridge.
screen: `THE CAR IN THE MIRROR.` → `ALONE AT ELEVEN AT NIGHT.` → `THREE THINGS ON A STICKY NOTE.`

segments.voice: Here's how Rabbi Judah ends his saying. Look at three things and you won't come into the grip of sin. Know what is above you: an eye that sees, an ear that hears, and all your deeds written in a book. An eye, an ear, a book. The first picture is being seen. The second is being heard, even the things you say under your breath, and that's the line we're carrying today. The third is being remembered: nothing you do simply vanishes. The prophet Malachi has a picture like this, of a book of remembrance written before God for the people who revere God and think about God's name. Now, this could sound like a security camera, something to make you nervous. But notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say an eye that punishes. It says an eye that sees. The same eye sees the kindness nobody else noticed, and the ear hears the quiet apology, and the book records the small good deed from yesterday too. Being seen can be a comfort as much as a warning. And there's a later reading, from Hasidic teachers, who played with the Hebrew words for know what is above you. They read them as know that what is above comes from you. What happens up there, they said, depends on what you do down here. Either way, the saying closes the gap between the public you and the eleven p.m. you. There's only one of you, and it's seen, heard, and remembered.
screen: `AN EYE, AN EAR, A BOOK.` · `SEEN, HEARD, REMEMBERED.` · `IT SEES THE GOOD TOO.` · `WHAT IS ABOVE COMES FROM YOU.` · then, large: `THE EAR HEARS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be seen, gently. Settle, and breathe. Imagine that everything about this moment is noticed, not by a camera, but by someone who wishes you well. Your posture. Your breath. The worry you're carrying. Let yourself be seen that way. Then think of one thing you'll do today when nobody's watching, and picture doing it as if they were. If you pray, you can remember that, in this teaching, God sees and hears. The bell holds the time.
An eye that sees. The first of Rabbi Judah's three: an eye that sees, an ear that hears, and all your deeds written in a book.
Your line: the ear hears. Today, notice what you say under your breath, and let it be something you wouldn't mind being heard. Day two hundred fifty.

howItsDone: The saying is studied as a reminder that private conduct matters as much as public conduct, and that being seen includes the good as well as the bad.

original.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: an eye that sees and an ear that hears.

trapdoor: what you thought: someone's always watching you.
what it means: you're seen, heard and remembered, in the good as much as the bad.
what a scholar hears: Hasidic teachers reread da mah lema'lah mimkha, know what is above you, as know that what is above is from you.

notes: The Hasidic rereading of 'da mah lema'lah mimkha' as 'know that what is above is from you' is widely attributed to early Hasidic masters (often the Maggid of Mezritch); confirm and decide whether to name a teacher.
'Know before whom you stand' above the ark: the phrase comes from Berakhot 28b; how common it is above arks is a general claim; confirm.
The reading of the eye as seeing good as well as bad is interpretive framing, not a claim about a specific commentator.
